analysis.one_liner: Strips wage, safety, and sidewalk/bike-path requirements from federally funded highway projects.
analysis.headline: A bill to waive federal rules, including construction wage requirements, on federally funded highway projects died in committee without a hearing or vote and drew no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have suspended nearly all federal requirements—including rules that federally funded highway construction pay the local prevailing wage—on highway projects for five years, with the Transportation Secretary keeping only rules tied to road durability and public or workplace safety. It would also have repealed federal requirements and funding authorizations for pedestrian walkways and bicycle facilities, and removed protections requiring alternatives when a highway project cuts off a walking or biking route. It was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be highway construction contractors, who could pay whatever wages they chose on federally funded projects instead of the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage, and likely bid lower on contracts. State highway agencies and driving-focused project schedules would also benefit from fewer pedestrian and bicycle obligations and faster project approvals.

how_it_helps.text: Suspends all federal requirements—including the prevailing-rate-of-pay rules under the Davis-Bacon Act—on federal-aid highway and highway safety construction projects for five years, keeping only rules the Transportation Secretary ties to road durability or public and workplace safety.
Repeals the statutory requirement that federal-aid highway projects not sever existing walking and biking routes or endanger nonmotorized traffic unless a reasonable alternative route exists.

Repeals the federal program authorizations for building pedestrian walkways and bicycle transportation facilities, and strikes the requirement that state transportation plans include accessible sidewalks and bike facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded highway projects would bear the cost of losing prevailing-wage protection, which generally keeps their pay at the local standard for similar work. Pedestrians, cyclists, children, older adults, and people with disabilities would lose dedicated federal funding and planning requirements for sidewalks, crosswalks, and bike paths, and lose protection when new highways cut off walking routes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Road construction workers, pedestrians, and cyclists

drawbacks.text: Suspending prevailing-wage rules would likely reduce take-home pay for the workers who build federally funded highways; prevailing-wage requirements are designed to keep federal construction pay at local market standards.

Repealing the pedestrian and bicycle authorizations and planning requirements would remove dedicated federal funding and mandates for sidewalks, crosswalks, and bike facilities, which serve people who do not or cannot drive, including children, older adults, and individuals with disabilities.

The bill defines safety narrowly, letting the Transportation Secretary decide which remaining federal rules count as protecting public or workplace safety, which could allow other environmental, contracting, and accountability rules to lapse without replacement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case was speed: fewer federal strings could move road projects faster and cut costs. But the savings to contractors and state agencies would come largely out of construction workers' wages and out of federal support for sidewalks and bike paths, and removing route-severance protections could leave communities physically cut off when highways are rebuilt. The trade-off favors contractors and driving convenience at the expense of workers and nondrivers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Randy Forbes introduced the bill on March 5, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, highway construction workers kept prevailing-wage protection and federal funding for sidewalks and bike facilities remained in place; contractors never received the wage savings the bill would have allowed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Highway workers and nondrivers kept existing rules

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Bill Shuster, R)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Highways and Transit Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors, so no party breakdown exists; the single sponsor was a Republican.

industries.note: Suspending prevailing-wage rules on federally funded projects would have let contractors pay below the local standard wage, cutting their labor costs at the direct expense of their workforce.
Workers on federal-aid highway jobs would have lost Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage protection for five years, lowering pay on publicly funded work.

The bill repeals the federal authorizations for walkway and bicycle facility construction and strikes the requirement that state plans include them, removing dedicated federal support for sidewalks and bike paths that serve nondrivers.
